notes.title: Mercedes-Benz
notes.body: The German luxury carmaker. A full plate becomes a license plate, the first car image in a song built on speed.

notes.title: Trix
notes.body: The General Mills cereal whose ads always end with the rabbit being told the cereal is only for children. He's too old for that now.

notes.title: Master Chief
notes.body: The armored super soldier who stars in Microsoft's Halo games. The name sets up the Halo lines that follow.

notes.title: Halo: Reach
notes.body: Bungie's 2010 prequel in the Halo series. He wants a halo, the kind angels wear, and the game's title tells you it's out of his grasp.

notes.title: Teena Marie
notes.body: The Motown singer and songwriter known as Lady T, whose biggest solo hit, from 1981, is named at the start of the next line. He splits her name in two to get there.
The hook is a chase. He's trying to get away, something is right behind him at full speed, and the title names how fast it's gaining.

notes.title: Fire and Desire
notes.body: The 1981 slow-jam duet by Rick James and Teena Marie, from his album Street Songs. The hook borrows its two big words right after the Teena Marie lines.

notes.title: Dexter's Laboratory
notes.body: The Cartoon Network show about a boy genius with a secret lab and a sister, Dee Dee, who keeps wrecking it. It leads straight into him at work in his own lab.

notes.title: FX
notes.body: The cable network behind shows like Atlanta and The Bear. Its name doubles as shorthand for special effects.

notes.title: Ex-Factor
notes.body: Lauryn Hill's 1998 breakup song from The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill. He borrows the plea from its chorus and its title in one line.

notes.title: Devonta Freeman
notes.body: The former Atlanta Falcons running back and two-time Pro Bowler, a Miami native who played at Florida State. His last name spells out what he wants to be.
The title comes back three times like an engine revving, then the song flips. Whatever had him locked up, he gets himself out and keeps the way out in his own hands.
At the end the decision gets handed back to him, by name, again and again. A song about running ends on him choosing, and the last words are about making peace with where he is.
